front: $q = mc\Delta T$ applies only when {{c1::no phase change occurs}}; during a phase change use {{c2::$q = mL$}}.
why: q = mcdT vs q = mL and multi-step heating problems are calculated every exam

front: A calorimetry trace climbs to a peak then drifts down. Why does the peak underestimate $\Delta T$, and what is the fix?
why: Calorimetry extrapolation correction is a secondary experimental detail

front: A constant-volume measurement gives {{c1::$\Delta U$}} while a constant-pressure measurement gives {{c2::$\Delta H$}}.
why: Constant-V gives dU, constant-P gives dH is a common calorimetry discrete

front: A label reads 200 Calories. Converted properly that is about {{c1::836 kJ}}.
why: Calorie vs calorie conversion is trivia-grade unit detail

front: A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is {{c1::negative}}; at equilibrium ΔG = {{c2::0}}.
why: dG < 0 spontaneous, dG = 0 at equilibrium: foundational, tested every exam

front: A reaction producing fewer moles of gas than it consumes has a {{c1::negative}} $\Delta S_{sys}$.
why: Predicting the sign of dS from moles of gas is asked essentially every exam

front: A spontaneous endothermic process must be driven by {{c1::a sufficiently positive $\Delta S$}} at {{c2::high enough temperature}}.
why: Endothermic yet spontaneous via TdS at high T is a common sign-analysis item

front: A substance with a high specific heat shows {{c1::a smaller}} temperature change for a given amount of heat absorbed.
why: High specific heat means smaller dT is a common qualitative calorimetry item

front: An exothermic reaction has a {{c1::negative}} $\Delta H$, and the {{c2::surroundings}} warm up.
why: Exothermic negative dH and warming surroundings is foundational, tested every exam

front: Anchor: at 25 degrees C, each factor of 10 in K corresponds to about {{c1::5.7 kJ/mol}} of $\Delta G^{\circ}$.
why: 5.7 kJ/mol per decade of K is an estimation anchor, secondary to the equation

front: Are bond breaking and bond forming endothermic or exothermic?
why: Bond breaking endothermic, forming exothermic underlies dH estimates every exam

front: ATP hydrolysis is quoted near $-30.5$ kJ/mol, but in a living cell it is closer to {{c1::$-50$ kJ/mol}} because {{c2::Q is far below 1}}.
why: ATP in-cell dG vs standard is biochem context, secondary here

front: Distinguish reversible from irreversible processes thermodynamically.
why: Reversible vs irreversible process definitions are secondary physics-thermo content

front: Enthalpy of reaction from bond energies equals:
why: Restates the bond-energy dH cards in this deck

front: Estimate $\Delta H$ from bond enthalpies and note the direction of the subtraction.
why: Bond-enthalpy dH estimate with correct subtraction direction is a common calculation

front: Exothermic vs exergonic: which word describes heat and which describes spontaneity?
why: Exothermic vs exergonic distinction is tested essentially every exam

front: For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on {{c1::temperature}}, so an isothermal process has $\Delta U = 0$ and {{c2::$q = -w$}}.
why: Ideal-gas isothermal/adiabatic/isochoric relations are common physics-thermo items

front: From formation enthalpies, $\Delta H_{rxn}$ is {{c1::products minus reactants}}, and $\Delta H_f$ of an element in its standard state is {{c2::zero}}.
why: dHrxn from formation enthalpies with elements at zero is calculated every exam

front: Give the calorimetry equation.
why: q = mcdT is the core calorimetry equation, used every exam

front: Give the Gibbs free energy equation.
why: dG = dH - TdS is the central equation of the section

front: Heat denaturation of a protein has positive $\Delta H$ and positive $\Delta S$. What does that combination predict?
why: Protein melting as +dH/+dS crossover is a common biochem application

front: Heat, temperature, and internal energy are three different quantities. Distinguish them.
why: Heat vs temperature vs internal energy distinction is supporting conceptual content

front: How do $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ differ, and when does the difference matter?
why: dH = dU + PdV and when the difference matters is a common discrete

front: How do cells drive thermodynamically unfavorable reactions?
why: Reaction coupling to ATP hydrolysis is a common thermo/biochem reasoning step

front: How do ionic charge and radius affect lattice energy?
why: Lattice energy vs charge and radius is secondary bonding content

front: How does a bomb calorimeter differ from a coffee-cup calorimeter?
why: Bomb vs coffee-cup calorimeter (dU vs dH, C vs mc) is a common discrete

front: How does a temperature change shift equilibrium differently from a pressure or concentration change?
why: Only temperature changes K; heat as reactant/product is asked essentially every exam

front: How does an exothermic reaction raise the entropy of the surroundings?
why: dS_surr = -dH/T explains temperature dependence of spontaneity; common reasoning step

front: If $\Delta G^{\circ}$ is exactly 0 then K equals {{c1::1}}, and a $\Delta G^{\circ}$ of only a few kJ/mol means K is {{c2::near 1}}.
why: Magnitude of dG vs K is supporting interpretation of the dG = -RT ln K card

front: If $\Delta G^\circ$ is positive, then $K$ is:
why: Positive dG means K < 1 is a common direct application

front: In $\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ} + RT\ln Q$, at equilibrium Q equals {{c1::K}} and $\Delta G$ equals {{c2::0}}.
why: dG = dG + RT ln Q with Q = K at equilibrium is used essentially every exam

front: In an adiabatic process the heat exchanged is {{c1::0}}, so the internal energy change equals {{c2::the work done}}.
why: Adiabatic q = 0, dU = w with compression heating is a common physics-thermo item

front: In an isochoric (constant volume) process the work is {{c1::0}} and all the heat goes into {{c2::internal energy}}.
why: Isochoric w = 0 largely restates the constant-volume calorimetry card

front: In coffee-cup calorimetry the reaction's heat is {{c1::the negative of}} the heat absorbed by the solution.
why: Sign flip for q_rxn is supporting detail for the coffee-cup calorimetry card

front: On a P-V diagram, work equals {{c1::the area under the curve}} and a closed cycle's net work equals {{c2::the enclosed area}}.
why: Work as area under a P-V curve is a common physics-thermo figure item

front: On a plot of $\Delta G$ versus temperature, the slope equals {{c1::$-\Delta S$}} and the intercept equals {{c2::$\Delta H$}}.
why: Reading dG vs T as a line is a secondary graphical interpretation

front: Protein folding lowers the chain's own entropy yet happens spontaneously. What drives it?
why: Hydrophobic effect driving protein folding is a frequent biochem thermo question

front: Relate $\Delta G^\circ$ to the equilibrium constant.
why: dG = -RT ln K is a core equation used in calculations every exam

front: Restate the second law in the form that resolves apparent violations.
why: Second law dS_universe > 0 resolving local ordering is asked essentially every exam

front: Specific heat is per {{c1::gram}}, molar heat capacity is per {{c2::mole}}, and heat capacity belongs to the whole object.
why: Specific vs molar vs total heat capacity is a supporting setup distinction

front: Standard conditions mean {{c1::1 atm}} pressure and 1 M solute concentrations, conventionally at {{c2::298 K}}.
why: Standard-state conditions and the degree symbol meaning are a common discrete

front: State functions depend only on {{c1::the initial and final states}}, while {{c2::heat and work}} are path functions.
why: State vs path functions is foundational and licenses Hess law; tested every exam

front: State Hess's law.
why: Hess law is tested on essentially every exam

front: State the first law with its sign convention.
why: First law with sign convention is foundational and tested every exam

front: State the third law and what it makes possible.
why: Third law and absolute entropies are rarely tested detail

front: The biochemical standard state differs from the chemical one mainly by fixing {{c1::pH 7}} instead of 1 M $H^{+}$.
why: Biochemical standard state at pH 7 is secondary context for biochem values

front: The crossover temperature where spontaneity flips is {{c1::$T = \Delta H/\Delta S$}}, the point where $\Delta G$ equals {{c2::0}}.
why: Crossover temperature T = dH/dS is a common sign-analysis calculation

front: The first law of thermodynamics states:
why: Restates the first law with the opposite sign convention; the fuller card is kept

front: Under Hess's law, reversing a reaction {{c1::flips the sign of $\Delta H$}} and doubling it {{c2::doubles $\Delta H$}}.
why: Reversing and scaling reactions in Hess law is a required calculation step

front: Water anchors: specific heat {{c1::4.184 J/g per degree C}} and heat of vaporization about {{c2::2260 J/g}}.
why: Water specific heat 4.184 and heat of vaporization are used in calculations

front: What decides whether dissolving a salt is exothermic or endothermic?
why: Lattice vs hydration energy for dissolution is a secondary application

front: What does a catalyst change, and what does it leave untouched?
why: Catalyst leaves dG, K and equilibrium unchanged is asked nearly every exam

front: What does a coffee-cup calorimeter measure, and how is the calculation set up?
why: Coffee-cup calorimetry measures dH; setup with q = -mcdT is a common calculation

front: What happens to work, temperature, and entropy when an ideal gas expands freely into a vacuum?
why: Free expansion into vacuum is a secondary physics-thermo scenario

front: What is a state function? Give examples.
why: Restates the state-function cloze card in this deck

front: What is the sign of $\Delta S$ for a gas condensing?
why: Restates the entropy-change cards in this deck

front: When is a reaction spontaneous at ALL temperatures?
why: dH/dS sign combinations and spontaneity at all temperatures is asked every exam

front: Which change has the largest positive $\Delta S$?
why: Vaporization as the largest entropy jump is a common ranking discrete

front: Which changes reliably increase entropy?
why: Reliable entropy-increasing changes, especially more gas moles, tested every exam

front: Which has the highest specific heat?
why: Restates the water specific-heat cards; trivia as a standalone

front: Which thermodynamic quantity determines the spontaneity of a reaction at constant temperature and pressure?
why: Restates the dG spontaneity cards in this deck

front: Why can one reaction be favorable inside a cell yet unfavorable at standard state?
why: In-cell vs standard favorability restates the dG = dG + RT ln Q card

front: Why does a negative $\Delta G$ say nothing about how fast a reaction runs?
why: Thermodynamics vs kinetics (spontaneous but slow) is tested essentially every exam

front: Why is $\Delta G = 0$ at a normal melting or boiling point?
why: dG = 0 at phase transitions and dS = dH/T is a common calculation shortcut

front: Why is $\Delta H_{vap}$ much larger than $\Delta H_{fus}$ for the same substance?
why: Why dHvap exceeds dHfus is supporting explanation

front: Why is a heating curve flat during melting and boiling?
why: Flat heating-curve plateaus during phase change are a common figure item
